guide.title: Testaccio, Rome: the ancient river port, the mountain of amphorae and the slaughterhouse quarter
guide.intro: Testaccio is R. XX, the twentieth of Rome's rioni by toponymic code, and it was carved out of Ripa in 1921. It covers about sixty hectares on the left bank of the Tiber, and it is a modern quarter standing on very old ground. The quay of Rome's ancient river port is set into the embankment wall; Monte Testaccio, an artificial hill 54 metres high and about a kilometre round, is built of the stacked sherds of the oil amphorae emptied at that port. Above them the city laid out a residential quarter from the end of the nineteenth century for the workers of the industries settling along the via Ostiense, and named its streets for engineers, printers, navigators and scientists: Volta, Galvani, Franklin, Manuzio, Bodoni, Ghiberti, Vespucci, Zabaglia. The slaughterhouse of 1888 to 1891 is now an arts campus, and the market moved into a new hall in 2012.

sections.heading: What is in Testaccio, and what is not
sections.body:
Several things a visitor would file under Testaccio stand in the rione next door, and the inventory of the Museo diffuso di Testaccio says so itself in two places: the Palazzo delle Poste on via Marmorata is in rione San Saba, and the Arco di San Lazzaro is in rione Ripa. Neither is written on this page. Nor is Porta San Paolo, nor the Museo della Via Ostiense housed inside it, nor the square in front of it, nor the stations around it; those belong to San Saba and to the quartiere Ostiense. The tomb of Servius Sulpicius Galba is a third case of the same shape. What stands on via Giovanni Branca is a museo diffuso panel telling the tomb's story; the tomb itself is at the Parco archeologico del Celio.

Via Marmorata is the clearest example of the problem. The street runs along the rione's edge, with Ripa at one end and San Saba at the other, and buildings addressed on it belong to three different rioni, so this guide uses it as an address and does not write it as a place. Piazza dell'Emporio, at the eastern landing of Ponte Sublicio, is Ripa's for the same reason and is not written here either.

Two things are written here despite standing on a shared line. The Pyramid of Cestius was taken into the Aurelian Walls as a bastion, and the walls carry a rione boundary; the Soprintendenza Speciale addresses the monument on the Testaccio side, at via Raffaele Persichetti, it.wikipedia files it under R. XX Testaccio, and the administration of the Non-Catholic Cemetery, which states its own address as being in the Rione di Testaccio, orients its visitors by the Pyramid as the thing on the other side of its wall. Ponte Sublicio is written here because Roma Capitale's tourism service states that the present bridge joins the rioni of Trastevere and Testaccio at Porta Portese.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Metro line B stops at Piramide, and every operator in the rione that publishes transport gives that station first. For the Pyramid of Cestius the Soprintendenza Speciale adds bus 23, 75, 280 and 716 and tram 3 and 8. The Non-Catholic Cemetery gives bus 3, 23, 30, 60, 75, 83, 95, 175 and 280 and the same metro station. The Mattatoio gives Metro B Piramide, tram 3 at Marmorata/Galvani, bus 719 at Galvani/Zabaglia and buses 170 and 781 at largo Marzi; the Città dell'Altra Economia, in the same complex, gives Metro B Piramide and bus 719, and has bike racks and a large car park.

Once you are in the rione, steer by addresses. Monte Testaccio is entered from via Nicola Zabaglia 24. The Non-Catholic Cemetery is at via Caio Cestio 6, and its own directions say that via Caio Cestio is a turning off via Marmorata on the north side of the Pyramid, with the entrance on the left halfway along the street. The Pyramid is entered from via Raffaele Persichetti. Roma Capitale's tourism service gives the Mattatoio as piazza Orazio Giustiniani 4, and the operator still uses the via Beniamino Franklin gate as the main entrance. The Nuovo Mercato Testaccio has entrances on via Beniamino Franklin, via Alessandro Volta, via Aldo Manuzio and via Lorenzo Ghiberti; the archaeological area beneath it is reached from inside the hall, with the assembly point at stall 63. The Emporium quay is on Lungotevere Testaccio, opposite no. 11. The Rome War Cemetery is on via Nicola Zabaglia. The fire brigade's museum is at via Galvani 2, with the barracks entrance at via Marmorata 15.

The street names themselves are a usable map. The rione's streets are dedicated to explorers, navigators, entrepreneurs, shipowners, engineers, scientists, publishers, printers and artists, which is why a walk here runs Volta, Galvani, Franklin, Manuzio, Bodoni, Ghiberti, Vespucci, Rubattino and Zabaglia.

sections.heading: Getting in to the ancient city
sections.body:
Almost all of Roman Testaccio is buried, built over or behind a gate, and each site has its own regime. Read them before you plan a day around any of them.

Monte Testaccio is opened by booking only, to groups bringing their own guide, up to thirty people a visit, on 060608 between 09.00 and 19.00. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina's tariff is 4.00 euro full and 3.00 euro reduced, free for residents of Rome and the metropolitan area on production of proof of residence and free for MIC card holders; the price does not include a guide. The same page advises low comfortable shoes, states that the site is not accessible to wheelchair users and that there are no toilets, and forbids approaching the edges of the hill, going onto the slopes and picking up sherds.

The Emporium, the ancient quay in the embankment wall, is described by Roma Capitale's tourism service as visitable only on extraordinary openings, which are booked through the Museo diffuso di Testaccio at sottosopra.testaccio@gmail.com. The horreum under the Nuovo Mercato is shown by the archaeologists who excavated it, in visits of about forty-five minutes for groups of up to twenty, free with an optional donation, on open days announced by the market's traders; the market states that visits are suspended while the spaces are refurbished. The Pyramid of Cestius opens on an announced cycle rather than daily: after works funded under the PNRR, the Soprintendenza Speciale announced openings between 4 September and 31 October 2026, with compulsory booking through Eventbrite, and outside announced openings the monument is not open to visitors.

The Porticus Aemilia asks nothing of you. Its piers stand between the apartment blocks of via Giovanni Branca, via Rubattino and via Florio, and the archaeological park around them, part of the museo diffuso, has entrances on via Rubattino and via Beniamino Franklin. The rione route of the museo diffuso itself is described by Roma Capitale as freely accessible, and seventeen of its panels stand in the rione.

faq.question: Is the Pyramid of Cestius in Testaccio, and can you go inside it?
faq.answer: It is written here as Testaccio's. The Soprintendenza Speciale gives its entrance as via Raffaele Persichetti, on the Testaccio side, it.wikipedia files it under R. XX Testaccio, and the Non-Catholic Cemetery, whose administration states that it is itself in the Rione di Testaccio, orients visitors by the monument. Going in depends on the calendar. After works funded under the PNRR the Soprintendenza Speciale announced a cycle of openings between 4 September and 31 October 2026: unguided daytime visits on 5, 12 and 19 September and 3, 10, 17, 24 and 31 October at 16.30, 17.30 and 18.30 for up to fifty people a turn; free guided evening visits on 4, 11, 18 and 25 September at 19.00, 20.00 and 21.00 for up to thirty; and openings for the European Heritage Days on 26 and 27 September, hourly from 10.00 to 16.00. Each visit runs forty-five minutes, booking through Eventbrite is compulsory, entry is free, and outside announced openings the monument is not open to visitors.

faq.question: Is Porta San Paolo in Testaccio?
faq.answer: No, and neither is the Museo della Via Ostiense inside the gate, nor piazza di Porta San Paolo, nor the 1943 memorial plaques, nor the metro and rail stations around them. The gate and its museum belong to rione San Saba, and the transport around piazzale Ostiense to the quartiere Ostiense. The it.wikipedia article on Testaccio lists the gate among the rione's archaeological sites, and this guide does not follow it.

faq.question: Can you climb Monte Testaccio?
faq.answer: Only on a booked visit. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina, which manages the hill, opens it to groups that bring their own guide, up to thirty people, with compulsory booking on 060608 between 09.00 and 19.00; individual visits are also possible by booking on a published calendar. The tariff is 4.00 euro full and 3.00 euro reduced, free for residents of Rome and the metropolitan area on production of proof of residence and free for MIC card holders, and it does not include a guide. The Sovrintendenza advises low comfortable shoes, states that the site is not accessible to wheelchair users and that there are no toilets, and forbids going onto the slopes, approaching the edges and picking up sherds.

faq.question: When is the Non-Catholic Cemetery open, and who is buried there?
faq.answer: Its administration gives Monday to Saturday 09.00 to 17.00, last admission 16.30, and Sundays and public holidays 09.00 to 13.00, last admission 12.30. It closes on 1 and 6 January, for fifteen days around Ferragosto, and on 8, 24, 25, 26 and 31 December, and closes at 13.00, last entry 12.30, at Easter and Easter Monday, on 25 April, 1 May and 2 and 29 June; it also cautions that it may close without notice for reasons beyond its control. It states that it does not at present offer guided visits, so groups bring their own guide and book a slot. It has been an active burial ground since 1716, holds over 6,000 burials representing more than fifty religious denominations from nearly sixty countries, and is the burial place of John Keats, Percy Bysshe Shelley, Antonio Gramsci, Carlo Emilio Gadda, Andrea Camilleri, Arnoldo Foà, August von Goethe and Hans von Marées.

faq.question: What was Campo Testaccio?
faq.answer: A football ground on via Nicola Zabaglia, now the Parco Testaccio. A.S. Roma played its home matches there from 3 November 1929 to 30 June 1940 — 161 matches, 103 won, 32 drawn, 26 lost. The engineer Silvio Sensi designed it on the model of British grounds, and Goodison Park in particular, with four wooden stands painted in the club's gold and Pompeian red, a capacity of 20,000 and a pitch whose dimensions could be adjusted. It was abandoned at the end of the 1939–40 season as obsolete and demolished that October.

faq.question: Where do you eat in Testaccio?
faq.answer: The covered market on via Lorenzo Ghiberti opens Monday to Saturday from 07.00 to 15.30 and describes itself as a hundred stalls, a hundred stories, a thousand products. Nine further addresses appear on this page, each written on what its own operator publishes: the delicatessen Volpetti on via Marmorata; the pasticcerie Barberini on via Marmorata and Linari on via Nicola Zabaglia; the trattorie Perilli on via Marmorata, Da Bucatino on via Luca della Robbia and Lo Scopettaro on Lungotevere Testaccio; Felice a Testaccio on via Mastro Giorgio; and, on via di Monte Testaccio, Checchino dal 1887 and Flavio al Velavevodetto. That is what this guide can honestly stand behind, and it is a fraction of what trades in the rione.

places.name: Monte Testaccio (Monte dei Cocci)
places.summary: An artificial hill of stacked amphora sherds between the Aurelian Walls and the left bank of the Tiber, made by the dumping of emptied oil amphorae from the river port. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina, which manages it and records its own field Rione: XX - Testaccio, gives the height as 54 metres and the circumference as about a kilometre. Visits are by booking only, for groups bringing their own guide, up to thirty people a turn, on 060608 between 09.00 and 19.00; individual visits are also possible by booking on a published calendar. The tariff is 4.00 euro full and 3.00 euro reduced, free for residents of Rome and the metropolitan area on production of proof of residence and free for MIC card holders, and it does not include a guide. The Sovrintendenza advises low comfortable shoes, states that the site is not accessible to wheelchair users and that there are no toilets, and forbids approaching the edges, going onto the slopes and picking up sherds.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina dates the tipping to between the Augustan period and the middle of the 3rd century AD. The material is testae, mostly amphora fragments: oil from Baetica left a residue that spoiled quickly, so the jars could not be reused and were broken and stacked in order. Lime was spread through the tip to control the smell of decomposition and has worked incidentally as a binder holding the hill together. A ramp and two cart tracks made the height possible. Many handles carry stamps and tituli picti recording the exporter, the contents, the checks made in transit and the consular date. From the medieval period the hill hosted the ludus Testacie, and in the nineteenth century the ottobrate; the rione article records a palio run here in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, from which the hill's other name, Mons de Palio.

places.name: Emporium, the ancient river port
places.summary: The quay of Rome's ancient river port, set into the modern embankment wall on Lungotevere Testaccio, opposite no. 11. About 500 metres of quay survive, 90 metres deep, with stairs, ramps and projecting travertine mooring blocks. Roma Capitale's tourism service states that it is visitable only on extraordinary openings; access forms part of the Museo diffuso di Testaccio, which takes bookings at sottosopra.testaccio@gmail.com.
places.history: Livy places the building of the Emporium in 193 BC, by the aediles Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Lucius Aemilius Paullus, and its paving in stone in 174 BC. Roma Capitale's tourism service dates the port to the 1st century AD. The two accounts are not reconciled here. Behind the travertine quay stood two ranges of warehouses fronting a cryptoporticus, with offices above. Goods landed at Ostia and Portus were brought here and redistributed: wine, grain, garum, and above all oil. The port peaked under Trajan in the 2nd century and was abandoned in the 4th, then buried, and in the Middle Ages the ground was used for burials. It was rediscovered from the end of the nineteenth century and excavated in 1868 to 1870, during the embankment works, and again in 1952. The marbles landed here gave via Marmorata its name, the street that connects the port of Ripa with Porta San Paolo; after the decline of Rome the unworked blocks lay as res nullius for centuries, an open-air quarry of part-worked stone.

places.name: Porticus Aemilia
places.summary: The remains of a very large Roman warehouse building, standing between the apartment blocks of via Giovanni Branca, via Rubattino and via Florio. The urban archaeological park around them belongs to the Museo diffuso di Testaccio, with entrances on via Rubattino and via Beniamino Franklin.
places.history: It was built in 193 BC by the aediles Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Lucius Aemilius Paullus and rebuilt in 174 BC by the censors Quintus Fulvius Flaccus and Aulus Postumius Albinus. It was raised in opus incertum in tufa, 487 metres long and 60 metres wide, on 294 piers making seven ranks and fifty vaulted aisles each 8.30 metres wide, covering 25,000 square metres about 90 metres back from the river. Piranesi engraved the remains in 1756. The identification is disputed and the dispute is not settled: a reading published in 2006 by Cozza and Tucci takes the building for republican navalia, sheds for the war fleet, and excavations from 2010 by the Soprintendenza with the Royal Netherlands Institute and Municipio I produced evidence supporting neither that identification nor the identification with the Porticus Aemilia named in the literary sources.

places.name: Area archeologica del Nuovo Mercato Testaccio
places.summary: Beneath the Nuovo Mercato Testaccio, in the market's own words, years of excavation and restoration brought to light the remains of a very old horreum, a Roman storage warehouse, which still holds hundreds of amphorae and other finds. The site is managed by the Soprintendenza Speciale Archeologia Belle Arti e Paesaggio di Roma. It is reached through the market on open days announced by its traders, in visits led by the archaeologists who excavated it, lasting about forty-five minutes for groups of up to twenty, free, with an optional donation. The assembly point is at stall 63. The market states that visits are suspended while the spaces are refurbished.
places.history: The horreum lies under the trading floor of the market hall the traders moved into in 2012, and is entered from inside it.

places.name: Piramide di Caio Cestio
places.summary: The tomb of Gaius Cestius, 36.40 metres high on a square base 29.50 metres a side, built into the line of the Aurelian Walls. Entry is free and is from via Raffaele Persichetti; the Soprintendenza Speciale names Barbara Rossi as the responsible official. After works funded under the PNRR, the Soprintendenza Speciale announced a cycle of special openings between 4 September and 31 October 2026: unguided daytime visits on 5, 12 and 19 September and 3, 10, 17, 24 and 31 October at 16.30, 17.30 and 18.30, for up to fifty people a turn; free guided evening visits on 4, 11, 18 and 25 September at 19.00, 20.00 and 21.00, for up to thirty; and openings for the European Heritage Days on 26 and 27 September, hourly from 10.00 to 16.00, for up to fifty. Each visit runs forty-five minutes. Booking is compulsory through Eventbrite. Outside announced openings the monument is not open to visitors. Metro B Piramide; bus 23, 75, 280 and 716; tram 3 and 8.
places.history: The Soprintendenza Speciale dates the tomb between 18 and 12 BC: the sumptuary law of 18 BC stopped the heirs placing valuable tapestries in the chamber, and Agrippa, named among the beneficiaries of the will, died in 12 BC. Cestius, a member of the priestly college of the epulones, required in his will that the work be finished in 330 days. The core is concrete faced with brick, with an outer skin of Luna marble. The burial chamber measures about 23 square metres, is barrel-vaulted and was walled up at the burial; it was frescoed in panels with nymphs alternating with lustral vases, and four winged Victories at the angles of the vault. The pyramid was taken as a bastion into the circuit built at Aurelian's initiative between 272 and 279. A medieval tunnel driven in from the north violated the tomb, and the cinerary urn was lost. In the Middle Ages the monument was identified as the meta Remi, paired with the meta Romuli, and Petrarch repeated the attribution. The excavations of Alexander VII, from 1660 to 1663, reopened the chamber and found it empty, recovered the two inscribed statue pedestals around 1662 and re-erected two corner columns; a project by Borromini to turn the chamber into a church came to nothing. A nineteenth-century lightning strike brought down the apex and a conductor was fitted. The chamber was restored in 2001 and a further restoration ran from 2012 to 2015. At the end of the PNRR intervention the Soprintendenza Speciale listed the access staircase made safe, the garden's planting surveyed and monitored, new lighting, and new interpretive and welcome panels for accessibility.

places.name: Cimitero Acattolico di Roma (Non-Catholic Cemetery)
places.summary: A walled burial ground whose administration gives its address as Via Caio Cestio, 6 nel Rione di Testaccio, 00153 Roma. It has been an active cemetery since 1716 and is privately managed and still in use; its historic garden holds over 6,000 burials, representing more than fifty religious denominations from nearly sixty countries. Opening is Monday to Saturday 09.00 to 17.00, last admission 16.30, and Sundays and public holidays 09.00 to 13.00, last admission 12.30. It closes on 1 and 6 January, for fifteen days around Ferragosto, and on 8, 24, 25, 26 and 31 December, and closes at 13.00, last entry 12.30, at Easter and Easter Monday, on 25 April, 1 May and 2 and 29 June; the administration also cautions that it may close without notice for reasons beyond its control. Groups must book, in fixed slots — Monday to Saturday at 10.00, 11.30, 14.00 and 15.30, Sundays and holidays at 10.00 and 11.00, none at All Saints — with at most two groups in the morning and two in the afternoon, capped at fourteen visitors plus one leader or licensed guide, and no booking is taken for groups under sixteen; a voluntary contribution of 5 euro a visitor is suggested. The cemetery states that it does not at present offer guided visits, so groups bring their own guide. There is a visitors' centre with volunteers, books and guides, there are toilets and a chapel, and a cat colony lives inside the walls. Its own directions say that via Caio Cestio is a turning off via Marmorata on the north side of the Pyramid and that the entrance is on the left halfway along; it also says the Pyramid is seen well from the old cemetery but cannot be entered from the garden. The administration notes that architectural barriers may affect some visitors' experience. Bus 3, 23, 30, 60, 75, 83, 95, 175 and 280; Metro B Piramide.
places.history: Burial in consecrated ground was closed to non-Catholics under the Papal States, and a ruling of the Holy Office in 1671 allowed non-Catholic gentlemen to be buried here rather than at the Muro Torto. The first recorded Protestant burial is that of William Arthur, a follower of the exiled James Stuart, who died in Rome in 1716; Francesco Valesio records the burial in 1732 of William Ellis, treasurer to the king of England, at the foot of the Pyramid. The official opening date given is 11 October 1821. A ditch was dug round the old part in 1824, and until 1870 crosses and inscriptions alluding to the Resurrection were forbidden; the older part was closed to burials in the 1820s and a walled enclosure added. Custody and management rest with the foreign missions in Italy, whose ambassadors take the presidency in annual rotation. John Keats and Percy Bysshe Shelley are buried here, as are Antonio Gramsci, Carlo Emilio Gadda, Andrea Camilleri, Arnoldo Foà, August von Goethe and Hans von Marées; the Angelo del dolore over the grave of Emelyn Story is by William Wetmore Story. Keats's stone reads 24 February, while Joseph Severn recorded the death at about eleven on the evening of 23 February 1821: the Roman civil day began at the evening Ave Maria. Camilleri's remains were brought here on 18 July 2019, and Giorgio Napolitano was buried on 26 September 2023.

places.name: Rome War Cemetery
places.summary: A Commonwealth war cemetery on via Nicola Zabaglia, established in 1947 and built by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission, which still manages and maintains it, as one of about fifty comparable sites in Italy, to a design by the architect Louis de Soissons. It is approached through an open circular vestibule sheltering a bronze box with the names of the dead; the headstones are aligned along the walls, the Stone of Remembrance stands at the centre of the rows, and a large stone cross closes the avenue facing the entrance. No wall separates it from the street, only a light railing. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: It was laid out on the state-owned strip of the old prati del popolo romano, between Monte Testaccio and the Aurelian Walls. It was made for the dead of the Rome garrison and later received bodies from the province, and airmen and soldiers who died in captivity, between 1939 and 1945.

places.name: Aurelian Walls, Testaccio segment
places.summary: The stretch of the Aurelian Walls that runs along viale del Campo Boario, named as a site of its own in the inventory of the Museo diffuso di Testaccio. Only this stretch is described here; the circuit runs on through many other units of the city.
places.history: The circuit was built at Aurelian's initiative between 272 and 279, and the Pyramid of Cestius was taken into it as a bastion. The Rome War Cemetery was laid out on the strip of the old prati del popolo romano between Monte Testaccio and this line of wall.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria Liberatrice
places.address: Piazza di Santa Maria Liberatrice, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: The parish church on piazza di Santa Maria Liberatrice, built between 1906 and 1908 to a design by the architect Mario Ceradini in a neo-Romanesque and neo-Byzantine manner. Inside, three aisles stand on columns whose capitals carry the symbols of the evangelists; the central band of the floor is a black-and-white mosaic with polychrome marble fragments, geometric motifs and the signs of the zodiac in panels. Between 1956 and 1964 Luciano Bartoli painted the apse fresco, of the Trinity, the Incarnation and the works of mercy below, and made the stained glass of the façade and the aisles.
places.history: Pius X entrusted the building first to the Benedictines and then definitively to the Salesians, who were already working in the quarter; the first parish priest was Luigi Maria Olivares, later bishop of Sutri and Nepi. In the same years the mayor Ernesto Nathan gave Domenico Orano the work of cultural and social provision in the rione. The pope transferred here the titulus of the demolished church of Santa Maria Liberatrice al Foro Romano, together with its venerated image, the fresco Sancta Maria libera nos a poenis inferni, which is slightly concave because it came from the old church's apse and had been kept after the demolition by the Oblates of Tor de' Specchi. The altar of the old church was moved here as well, and the mosaic on the façade reproduces one of its decorations.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria della Divina Provvidenza a Testaccio
places.summary: A neo-Baroque church on via Alessandro Volta, built between 1887 and 1889 and consecrated in 1889, in a complex that also fronted via Galvani and via Nicola Zabaglia. On the lower storey of the façade four Doric pilasters flank the portal, which is crowned by an arched pediment. The complex closed in 2008 and the diocese no longer lists the church, which cannot be entered; it is written here as streetscape.
places.history: Two attributions stand in the sources and neither is set aside here: the architect Antonio Lenti, and Mariano Armellini's Le chiese di Roma dal secolo IV al XIX of 1891, which says the church was begun in 1888 to the designs of signor Barbiellini. It was built for the Figlie della Divina Provvidenza, a congregation founded in 1832 by Maria Elena Bettini to educate poor girls, with the support of the Barnabites of San Carlo ai Catinari. The complex held a canteen, an orphanage and a school, and the church served the new quarter before the parish of Santa Maria Liberatrice existed. The convent was the congregation's mother house until the end of the twentieth century, when it moved to via Matteo Bartoli 255.

places.name: Le madonnelle di Testaccio
places.summary: Wayside shrines set at street corners in the rione. Roma Capitale's tourism service describes the one at a corner of piazza Testaccio: it is a copy of an old seventeenth-century image once kept in the church of Santa Maria Liberatrice al Foro Romano and placed in 1908 on the altar of the Testaccio church of the same name. Further shrines stand elsewhere in the rione; only this one is described here.
places.history: The image it copies belongs to the same transfer that carried the titulus of the demolished church at the Roman Forum to the new parish church in Testaccio.

places.name: Mattatoio di Roma
places.summary: The city's former slaughterhouse, now an exhibition and arts campus on the block bounded by via Beniamino Franklin, which is still the main entrance, Lungotevere Testaccio, via Aldo Manuzio and viale del Campo Boario. Roma Capitale's tourism service gives the address as piazza Orazio Giustiniani 4. Hours are 11.00 to 20.00, last admission 19.30, closed Mondays, and it opens only when an exhibition is running. Metro B Piramide; tram 3 at Marmorata/Galvani; bus 719 at Galvani/Zabaglia and 170 and 781 at largo Marzi.
places.history: In the operator's own words it was built between 1888 and 1891 by Gioacchino Ersoch. The engineer Filippo Laccetti worked on the project and devised a system for disposing of offal into the Tiber. It covers 25,000 square metres and is of the pavilion type, laid out on a geometric plan with the slaughter halls flanking the main avenue and the pig and offal work pushed to the periphery, on what is now via Manuzio. It was decommissioned in 1975 and replaced by a plant at Tor Sapienza. The restoration grew from an idea of Zoneattive in the early 2000s, and site works ran from 2006 to 2010 on the water-tank pavilions, the pelanda and the pig slaughterhouse. In 2000 pavilion 7 on via Aldo Manuzio and the pavilions along via Beniamino Franklin were converted into lecture rooms for the architecture faculty of Università Roma Tre, and the Accademia di Belle Arti also occupies part of the complex. In 2002 pavilions 9a and 9b went to MACRO for contemporary art, first as Macro Future and then as Macro Testaccio. Musei in Comune managed the site until 2017; since 2018 a significant part has been managed for Roma Capitale by Azienda Speciale Palaexpo. One scheme that would have removed it came to nothing: Ponte Testaccio, begun in 1938, was to have been carried on towards Trastevere station by demolishing the slaughterhouse, and the demolition never took place.

places.name: La Pelanda
places.summary: A performance and production space of about 5,000 square metres inside the Mattatoio, used for dance, research theatre, music, installation work, workshops and production residencies. The restoration kept the structures and fittings of the Galleria delle Vasche; the main body is a large nave with a truncated-cone chimney and its metal plant, and the conversion was designed as an open, modular, walk-through system with large glazed surfaces. It also holds the Aula Studio La Pelanda, a free study room.
places.history: The pelanda was one of the buildings taken in hand in the site works of 2006 to 2010, within the recovery of the Mattatoio complex.

places.name: Città dell'Altra Economia
places.summary: A market and events space in the Campo Boario of the former Mattatoio, occupying 3,500 square metres recovered from the old Pese del Bestiame, the livestock weighbridge, and from the canopies and shelters of the Campo Boario. It holds organic-agriculture and fair-trade markets, training workshops, concerts and festivals, and contains a bio-bar and a bio-restaurant. Its hours are Tuesday to Sunday, 07.30 to 24.00. There are bike racks and a large car park; Metro B Piramide and bus 719.
places.history: The buildings were restored conservatively on bioarchitecture principles, within the wider recovery of the Mattatoio, and the space opened in 2007. The operator states that it holds more than a hundred events a year.

places.name: Scuola Popolare di Musica di Testaccio
places.summary: A music school in the former Mattatoio, with its own concert room, the Sala Giovanna Marini. It is still working: enrolment for 2026/27 is open and concerts are listed in the Sala Giovanna Marini. Its library, founded in 1983, holds over 9,000 titles together with the Fondo Furlan of eighteenth- and nineteenth-century manuscripts.
places.history: The school was founded in 1975 on the initiative of Bruno Tommaso with other Roman musicians, among them Martin Joseph, Tony Ackerman, Maurizio Giammarco, Giancarlo Schiaffini, Eugenio Colombo, Giovanna Marini, Michele Iannaccone and Danilo Terenzi; early activity was partly hosted at the Teatro Spazio Zero. Residents of the rione had priority in enrolment and free access to some workshops. There were 147 students enrolled and 20 teachers before teaching began, about 250 by the end of the first term, which ran from 1 March to 30 June 1975, and within two years a cap of 450 was imposed for want of space. In 1983 Giovanna Marini's Il Regalo dell'Imperatore went on a European tour.

places.name: Nuovo Mercato Testaccio
places.summary: The rione's covered market, open Monday to Saturday from 07.00 to 15.30, with entrances from via Beniamino Franklin, via Alessandro Volta, via Aldo Manuzio and via Lorenzo Ghiberti; the registered office is on via Lorenzo Ghiberti. The operator describes the hall in its own words as 100 banchi, 100 storie, 1000 prodotti — a hundred stalls, a hundred stories, a thousand products. The archaeological area beneath the trading floor is written separately.
places.history: The market moved here from piazza Testaccio in 2012, a date given independently by Roma Capitale's tourism service, by the Sovrintendenza Capitolina on its page for the Fontana delle Anfore, and by the rione article. Inti-Illimani recorded a song called El mercado Testaccio on their 1981 album Palimpsesto.

places.name: Volpetti
places.summary: A delicatessen at via Marmorata 47 selling cured meats, cheeses, baked goods and wine.
places.history: The business keeps a second address in the rione, trading as Volpetti Più.

places.name: Pasticceria Barberini
places.summary: A pasticceria and bar on via Marmorata, open Monday to Saturday from 06.00 to 21.00 and on Sunday from 06.00 to 20.00. Telephone 06 5725 0431.
places.history: The pasticceria bakes with lievito madre, natural leaven, and names its suppliers on its own site, among them Dallagiovanna flours, Valrhona chocolate and Bourbon vanilla.

places.name: Pasticceria Linari
places.summary: A pasticceria and bar on via Nicola Zabaglia, open every day from 06.30 to 21.30, and on Tuesday from 06.30 to 13.30. Telephone 06 5782358.
places.history: The business gives its registered name and address as Linari Roma S.r.l., via Nicola Zabaglia 9, 00153 Roma.

places.name: Checchino dal 1887
places.address: Via di Monte Testaccio 30, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: A restaurant on via di Monte Testaccio, open Wednesday to Sunday, lunch 12.30 to 15.00 and dinner 19.30 to 23.00, closed Monday and Tuesday; it opens on its closing days for exclusive bookings of at least thirty people.
places.history: The kitchen works in the tradition of the quinto quarto, the offal cuts that came out of the slaughterhouse. Dishes named on the restaurant's own site include insalata di zampi, rigatoni con la pajata, rigatoni al sugo di coda and coda alla vaccinara.

places.name: Felice a Testaccio
places.summary: A restaurant on via Mastro Giorgio, open every day, lunch 12.30 to 15.30 and dinner 19.00 to 23.30.
places.history: The kitchen finishes its cacio e pepe at the table. The group behind it opened a room in Milan in 2017 and one in Turin in 2024.

places.name: Trattoria Perilli
places.summary: A trattoria on via Marmorata. Telephone 06 5755100 or 06 5742415. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The restaurant's own page carries a poem about the place by Checco Durante.

places.name: Da Bucatino
places.address: Via Luca della Robbia 84/86, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: A restaurant on via Luca della Robbia, open Tuesday to Sunday from 12.15 to 15.00 and from 19.00 to 23.55. Telephone 06 5746886.
places.history: The restaurant occupies nos. 84 and 86 of via Luca della Robbia.

places.name: Flavio al Velavevodetto
places.address: Via di Monte Testaccio 97, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: A restaurant on via di Monte Testaccio. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: It belongs to a group that also runs Velavevodetto ai Quiriti, at piazza dei Quiriti 4/5, and two rooms in Milan.

places.name: Lo Scopettaro
places.summary: A trattoria on Lungotevere Testaccio, at no. 7. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The restaurant trades under the name Lo Scopettaro and gives its own address as Lungotevere Testaccio 7.

places.name: L'Alibi
places.address: Via di Monte Testaccio 40/44, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: An LGBTQIA+ club on via di Monte Testaccio, run as a cultural association with ARCO membership. Telephone +39 380 8980243. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The club gives its own address as via di Monte Testaccio 40/44, on the flank of the hill.

places.name: Teatro Vittoria
places.address: Piazza di Santa Maria Liberatrice 10, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: A prose theatre on piazza di Santa Maria Liberatrice, with 560 red velvet seats and a bar. Telephone 06 5781960; tickets are sold through Vivaticket. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale's tourism service records that from the early twentieth century the Vittoria was Testaccio's theatre: a two-storey building on an unpaved square, doing variety. It was demolished after the war and replaced by a block of flats whose ground floor held a cinema built by the exhibitor Amati; the cinema closed at the end of the 1970s. Conversion works to a prose theatre began in May 1986, commissioned by Attilio Corsini of the Attori & Tecnici cooperative from the architect Enrico Nespega, and the theatre opened in December 1986 with 560 red velvet seats. Corsini died in 2008. Rumori fuori scena is the cooperative's signature production.

places.name: Teatro di Documenti
places.summary: A theatre on via Nicola Zabaglia that sells guided visits of its own building, advertised as Visita del Teatro and Visita Spettacolo, and runs a programme for schools. Telephone 06 455 485 78. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The theatre receives support under POR FESR Lazio 2021-2027.

places.name: Multisala Greenwich
places.address: Via Giovanni Battista Bodoni 59, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: A cinema on via Giovanni Battista Bodoni, operated together with the Cinema Mignon under a single booking site.
places.history: The Greenwich and the Mignon share one ticketing service.

places.name: Museo Storico dei Vigili del Fuoco
places.summary: The historical museum of the Rome fire brigade, at via Galvani 2, with the barracks entrance at via Marmorata 15. It was inaugurated on 18 April 2002 and covers the development of rescue in the city from antiquity onwards. It is visitable by appointment only: ufficiostampa.roma@vigilfuoco.it, telephone 06 46722237; the museum's own telephone is 06 5781495.
places.history: The corps' own account describes scenographic reconstructions of the fire of AD 64, of the fire of 847 that came close to taking St Peter's, of the Sack of Rome in 1527 and of the bombing of Rome on 19 July 1943; sections on today's specialisms, among them divers, helicopter crews and the speleo-alpine-fluvial service; two reconstructions with audio and effects, of a flat fire and of a collapse after an earthquake; a multimedia room; and a laboratory bench for combustion experiments. Roma Capitale's tourism service adds that the collection was transferred here from the Scuola Antincendi at Capannelle.

places.name: Caserma dei Vigili del Fuoco Alberto De Jacobis
places.summary: The fire station at the corner of via Marmorata and via Luigi Galvani, designed by the architect Vincenzo Fasolo on a semicircular plan. The via Marmorata front has seven large doorways with flat arches, separated by rusticated pilasters whose capitals carry a fireman's helmet; the entrance at no. 15 is up seven steps between two plaques; the windows on this side are topped by a badge of a sword crossed with an axe; and a square tower on corbels rises over the internal courtyard.
places.history: The barracks was inaugurated on 28 October 1929. The sources do not agree on when it was built, giving three different spans and agreeing only on the inauguration, so no construction span is given here. It is named for the vice-brigadier Alberto De Jacobis, killed on 10 September 1943 during the German occupation of Rome, and has carried the dedication since 1994.

places.name: Museo diffuso di Testaccio
places.summary: A distributed museum rather than a building: a route across the rione created by the Soprintendenza Speciale Archeologia Belle Arti e Paesaggio di Roma, with teaching panels, a play-and-learn area for children, and bookable access to the Emporium, the Porticus Aemilia archaeological park and the archaeological area under the Nuovo Mercato. Roma Capitale's tourism service describes the rione route as freely accessible; bookings for the enclosed sites go to sottosopra.testaccio@gmail.com. Seventeen of its panels stand in the rione.
places.history: The route covers much of the rione's roughly 60 hectares, a figure the market's own site repeats. Its inventory also names buildings that stand outside Testaccio and says so: the Palazzo delle Poste on via Marmorata is in rione San Saba and the Arco di San Lazzaro is in rione Ripa. What stands on via Giovanni Branca is a panel telling the story of the tomb of Servius Sulpicius Galba, and not the tomb, which is at the Parco archeologico del Celio.

places.name: Piazza Testaccio
places.summary: A paved square with the Fontana delle Anfore at its centre, restyled in 2015 with new paving and street furniture. A madonnella stands at one of its corners.
places.history: The rione was instituted in 1921. In 1905 the Comitato per il miglioramento economico e morale di Testaccio obtained the assignment of a cleared lot on which the square was made, then named piazza Mastro Giorgio. The district market was held here for many years, until it moved to via Galvani in 2012; the fountain was returned to the centre of the square in the restyling that followed. A plaque of 2015 marks the birthplace of the singer Gabriella Ferri and reads: "Qui è nata / Gabriella Ferri / Grande interprete della canzone italiana".

places.name: Fontana delle Anfore
places.summary: A travertine fountain at the centre of piazza Testaccio, circular on a two-step base and surmounted by a tall pinnacle of massed amphorae. Four elongated basins radiate from the base, each carrying the arms of the Comune crowned by a ram's head, and their arched outer ends carry amphorae in low relief.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina, which owns the fountain, records that in 1924 the Comune held a national competition for five fountains in newly built quarters, and that the architect Pietro Lombardi (1894-1984) won the commission for piazza Mastro Giorgio, today piazza Testaccio. The fountain was inaugurated on 26 October 1927. Ground settlement soon appeared; in 1932 the administration proposed moving it to piazza dell'Emporio, Lombardi consented in 1933, and the rebuilding works ran in 1935. Within the redevelopment of piazza Testaccio that moved the market in 2012, the fountain was brought back: over 350 constituent blocks were dismantled, transported, restored and reassembled, each checked and numbered; a modern hydraulic system restored and reactivated the 45 water nozzles, long inactive; and lighting was installed inside the four rectangular basins for the first time. It was re-inaugurated on 24 January 2015. Lombardi made a series of rione fountains for the same competition, of which this is the Testaccio one.

places.name: Fontana di Pio IX in Lungotevere Testaccio
places.summary: A fountain set into the parapet of the embankment wall, aligned with via Florio, in white marble, travertine and brick facing. A brick front is framed by two rusticated travertine pilasters topped by spheres and flanked by volutes; above it the Mastai Ferretti arms sit between two festoons; a lion's-head spout feeds a third-century AD strigillated sarcophagus, and six travertine bollards stand round it. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina's page for it carries its own field, Rione: Testaccio.
places.history: It was made in 1939 and 1940 by Antonio Muñoz (1884-1960), to close the vista along the street. The 1869 plaque and the papal arms, which had faced the river, were moved into the parapet and joined to the ancient sarcophagus with new work; the plaque commemorates the excavations commissioned by Pius IX and carried out in the area by the archaeologist Pietro Ercole Visconti in 1868 and 1869. The fountain was restored in 1993 and again in 2000, after vandalism.

places.name: Fontana del Boccale
places.summary: A small fountain standing in a masonry exedra on via Nicola Zabaglia, shaped as a tankard in a circular basin, in red Vicenza marble on salvaged material from the area.
places.history: it.wikipedia dates the fountain to 1931 and attributes it to Raffaele De Vico, citing rerumromanarum and Roma Segreta; that attribution is given here as it.wikipedia's.

places.name: Piazza di Santa Maria Liberatrice and the Giardino Famiglia Di Consiglio
places.address: Piazza di Santa Maria Liberatrice, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: A square carrying the parish church of Santa Maria Liberatrice and the Teatro Vittoria, with a large planted garden at its centre, the Giardino Famiglia Di Consiglio.
places.history: The garden is named for the Di Consiglio family, murdered at the Fosse Ardeatine. Six of them were killed. Alessandro Portelli, in L'ordine è già stato eseguito (Rome 1999, p. 159), lists them: a boy of sixteen, one of seventeen, one of nineteen, one of twenty-one, the father, and the grandfather, Mosè, born in 1870. They were Testaccio traders, hawkers and butchers.

places.name: Parco Testaccio (ex Campo Testaccio)
places.summary: A public park on via Nicola Zabaglia, on the ground of Campo Testaccio, the football pitch where A.S. Roma played its home matches from 3 November 1929 to 30 June 1940.
places.history: The club played 161 matches here, winning 103, drawing 32 and losing 26. The ground was designed by the engineer Silvio Sensi on the model of British grounds, and of Goodison Park in particular: four wooden stands painted in the club's gold and Pompeian red, a capacity of 20,000, a grass pitch whose dimensions could be adjusted, and the manager's house on the site with a giant club badge painted on its outside wall. It cost 1,530,000 lire and average attendance was about 10,000. Tickets ran from 5 to 6 lire for the popolari to 30 to 35 for the covered stand, with half price for women, dopolavoristi, soldiers and university students and a 2-lire balilla rate; those without tickets watched from the top of Monte dei Cocci on the via Zabaglia side, where the roof of the stand hid half the pitch. Rugby Roma played here for two seasons, from 1937 to 1939, and the ground held one Italy rugby international. It was abandoned at the end of the 1939-40 season as obsolete and demolished that October. The 5-0 win over Juventus on 15 March 1931 lies behind the film Cinque a zero and the nickname Roma testaccina; the derby of 1 November 1933 is the other match the club's history remembers.

places.name: Via di Monte Testaccio and the grottini
places.address: Via di Monte Testaccio, 00153 Roma RM
places.summary: The street that runs round the base of Monte Testaccio. Caves, the grottini, were cut into the foot of the hill and used as cellars and stables; Roma Capitale's tourism service says they have become the restaurants and disco-pubs that make the night life along here. Which businesses hold them changes, and none is listed on this page.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the clay of the hill keeps the caves at about 10 degrees Celsius the year round, and that they held taverns from the Middle Ages.

places.name: Ponte Sublicio
places.summary: A bridge over the Tiber of three masonry arches, 105 metres long and 20 metres wide. Roma Capitale's tourism service states that the present Ponte Sublicio joins the rioni of Trastevere and Testaccio at Porta Portese. Its eastern landing, piazza dell'Emporio, is in rione Ripa.
places.history: The bridge was built between 1914 and 1917 to a design by Marcello Piacentini and inaugurated on 21 April 1919. It carries the name of the ancient pons Sublicius, which was a different structure.

places.name: Il Quartiere Moderno, the planned quarter of Testaccio
places.summary: The rione read as a piece of planning, and one of the subjects the Museo diffuso explains on its panels: a residential quarter built from the end of the nineteenth century for the workers of the industries settling along the via Ostiense. Its streets are dedicated to explorers, navigators, entrepreneurs, shipowners, engineers, scientists, publishers, printers and artists — Volta, Galvani, Franklin, Manuzio, Bodoni, Ghiberti, Vespucci, Rubattino, Zabaglia — which is a workable key to walking it.
places.history: Testaccio was detached in 1921 from the large and thinly populated rione Ripa, and Roma Capitale's tourism service gives 1921 for the rione's institution as well. The first master plan of the capital, in 1873, had already placed industrial expansion in the Ostiense area, favoured by flat ground, the via Ostiense, the river port and the railway. The rione's arms are recorded by Carlo Pietrangeli, in Insegne e stemmi dei rioni di Roma, Capitolium XXVIII/6, 1953, p. 190, as "Di rosso all'anfora d'oro", gules an amphora or. The school building on via Alessandro Volta, now the Istituto Comprensivo Elsa Morante, was built between 1920 and 1923 to a design by the architect Augusto Antonelli.

places.name: Casa di Elsa Morante
places.summary: A house in the rione carrying a plaque placed in 2004, recording that the writer Elsa Morante lived here. Its text reads "In questa casa ha abitato una straordinaria scrittrice italiana / Elsa Morante". A Stolperstein is set into the pavement in front of it.
places.history: Many episodes of Elsa Morante's novel La Storia are set in Testaccio, and Paola Cortellesi's film C'è ancora domani, of 2023, is set in the rione.

entries.name: Monte Testaccio
entries.note: An artificial hill 54 metres high, built of the broken oil amphorae unloaded at the river port between the Augustan period and the middle of the 3rd century AD; visits are by booking only, for groups with their own guide.

entries.name: Piramide di Caio Cestio
entries.note: The tomb of Gaius Cestius, 36.40 metres high on a base 29.50 metres a side, finished in 330 days under the terms of his will and later taken into the Aurelian Walls as a bastion.

entries.name: Cimitero Acattolico di Roma
entries.note: A burial ground active since 1716, holding over 6,000 graves from more than fifty religious denominations, among them those of Keats, Shelley and Gramsci.

entries.name: Emporium, the ancient river port
entries.note: About 500 metres of travertine quay survive in the embankment wall, with stairs, ramps and projecting mooring blocks; Roma Capitale says it can be visited only on extraordinary openings.

entries.name: Porticus Aemilia
entries.note: Piers of a warehouse 487 metres long stand between the apartment blocks; whether it is the Porticus Aemilia of the literary sources or a set of republican navalia is still argued.

entries.name: Mattatoio di Roma
entries.note: The slaughterhouse Gioacchino Ersoch built between 1888 and 1891, 25,000 square metres of pavilions, decommissioned in 1975 and now an exhibition campus open when a show is running.

entries.name: Fontana delle Anfore
entries.note: Pietro Lombardi's travertine fountain of massed amphorae, inaugurated on 26 October 1927, moved away in 1935 and brought back to the square block by block in 2015.

entries.name: Parco Testaccio
entries.note: The ground where A.S. Roma played 161 home matches between 1929 and 1940, with four wooden stands in gold and Pompeian red and a free view from the top of Monte dei Cocci.

entries.name: Nuovo Mercato Testaccio
entries.note: The covered market, open Monday to Saturday from 07.00 to 15.30, with four entrances and, beneath the trading floor, the remains of a Roman horreum.

entries.name: Checchino dal 1887
entries.note: A restaurant on via di Monte Testaccio cooking the quinto quarto, with rigatoni con la pajata and coda alla vaccinara on its own list; closed Monday and Tuesday.

entries.name: Felice a Testaccio
entries.note: Open every day on via Mastro Giorgio, for lunch from 12.30 and dinner from 19.00; the cacio e pepe is finished at the table.

entries.name: Volpetti
entries.note: A delicatessen at via Marmorata 47 selling cured meats, cheeses, baked goods and wine.

entries.name: Via di Monte Testaccio
entries.note: The road round the foot of the hill, where caves cut for cellars and stables, held at about 10 degrees Celsius by the clay, now hold restaurants and clubs.

entries.name: Museo diffuso di Testaccio
entries.note: Seventeen teaching panels set across the rione by the Soprintendenza Speciale, freely accessible, with bookings for the enclosed sites at sottosopra.testaccio@gmail.com.
